parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the equation of the tangent to the graph of \(f\) at \(x = 1\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the \(x\)-coordinates of the stationary points of \(f\).

idea: Product rule: \((uv)' = u'v + uv'\). Chain rule: the derivative of \(e^{-0.5x}\) is \(-0.5e^{-0.5x}\). Since \(e^{-0.5x}\) is never 0, \(f'(x) = 0\) only when the bracket is 0.

stem: The output of a solar water heater depends on the temperature difference \(T\) °C between the panel and the air. A model for its efficiency is \(E(T) = \dfrac{50T}{T^{2} + 400}\), for \(T > 0\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the quotient rule to show that \(E'(T) = \dfrac{50(400 - T^{2})}{(T^{2} + 400)^{2}}\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find the temperature difference that gives the greatest efficiency, and justify that it is a maximum.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the greatest efficiency.

idea: Quotient rule: \(\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)' = \dfrac{u'v - uv'}{v^{2}}\). The denominator of \(E'\) is always positive, so the sign of \(E'\) is the sign of \(400 - T^{2}\).

solution.label: b
steps: For \(T < 20\), \(E' > 0\); for \(T > 20\), \(E' < 0\). So \(E\) increases then decreases.
solution.answer: \(T = 20\) °C; \(E'\) changes from positive to negative there

stem: A company's monthly profit, \(P\) thousand dollars, when it spends \(x\) thousand dollars on advertising is modelled by \(P(x) = -x^{3} + 18x^{2} + 60x - 200\), for \(0 \le x \le 15\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find \(P'(x)\) and \(P''(x)\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the point of inflection of the graph of \(P\), and explain what it means for the company.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write down the interval on which the graph of \(P\) is concave up.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the advertising spend that gives the greatest profit.

idea: At a point of inflection \(P''\) changes sign. There \(P'\), the extra profit from each extra thousand dollars of advertising, is greatest: after it, each extra dollar is worth less (the ‘point of diminishing returns’).

solution.label: b
steps: \(P''(x) = 0\) at \(x = 6\), and \(P''\) changes from positive to negative there. \(P(6) = -216 + 648 + 360 - 200 = 592\).
\(P'(6) = 168\), the greatest rate of increase of profit.
solution.answer: \((6, 592)\): spending beyond $6000 still raises profit, but by less and less each time

solution.label: d
steps: \(P'(x) = 0\): \(x^{2} - 12x - 20 = 0\), so \(x = 6 + \sqrt{56} = 13.48\ldots\) (the other root is negative); \(P''\) is negative there.

stem: After a car goes over a bump, the vertical displacement of its body, \(y\) cm, \(t\) seconds later is modelled by \(y = e^{-0.2t}\sin t\), for \(0 \le t \le 2\pi\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that \(\dfrac{dy}{dt} = e^{-0.2t}(\cos t - 0.2\sin t)\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that \(\dfrac{d^{2}y}{dt^{2}} = e^{-0.2t}(-0.96\sin t - 0.4\cos t)\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the times at which \(y\) has a local maximum and a local minimum, and use part (b) to classify them.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the times of the points of inflection of the graph of \(y\).

idea: Stationary points need \(\cos t - 0.2\sin t = 0\), that is \(\tan t = 5\); points of inflection need \(-0.96\sin t - 0.4\cos t = 0\). In each case \(e^{-0.2t} \ne 0\), and \(\tan t = k\) has two solutions in \([0, 2\pi]\), \(\pi\) apart.

solution.label: a
steps: Product rule with \(\dfrac{d}{dt}e^{-0.2t} = -0.2e^{-0.2t}\): \(\dfrac{dy}{dt} = -0.2e^{-0.2t}\sin t + e^{-0.2t}\cos t\)

solution.label: d
steps: \(\tan t = -\dfrac{0.4}{0.96} = -\dfrac{5}{12}\): \(t = \pi - 0.3947\ldots = 2.746\ldots\) or \(t = 2\pi - 0.3947\ldots = 5.888\ldots\); \(\dfrac{d^{2}y}{dt^{2}}\) changes sign at each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use similar triangles to show that \(s = \dfrac{3x}{7}\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the rate at which the shadow is getting longer.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the speed at which the tip of the shadow is moving.

idea: The big triangle (post) and the small triangle (person) share the angle at the tip of the shadow. Differentiate the relation with respect to time, using \(\dfrac{dx}{dt} = 1.2\).

solution.label: c
steps: The tip is \(x + s = \dfrac{10x}{7}\) from the post: \(\dfrac{10}{7} \times 1.2\).

stem: A camera on the ground is 50 m from a launch pad and tracks a model rocket that rises vertically. When the rocket is 120 m high, it is rising at 20 m s⁻¹. Let \(h\) m be the height of the rocket and \(\theta\) the angle of elevation of the camera.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the rate at which \(\theta\) is increasing at that moment, in radians per second.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the rate at which the distance from the camera to the rocket is increasing at that moment.

idea: \(\tan\theta = \dfrac{h}{50}\). Differentiate both sides with respect to \(t\): \(\sec^{2}\theta\,\dfrac{d\theta}{dt} = \dfrac{1}{50}\dfrac{dh}{dt}\). For the distance, \(d^{2} = 50^{2} + h^{2}\).

stem: Answer this question without a calculator.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find \(\displaystyle\int e^{3x - 1}\,dx\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find \(\displaystyle\int \dfrac{x}{x^{2} + 4}\,dx\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the exact value of \(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/6} \cos 3x\,dx\).

idea: Reverse the chain rule. Differentiating \(e^{3x - 1}\) gives \(3e^{3x - 1}\), so divide by 3. The numerator \(x\) is half the derivative of \(x^{2} + 4\), which suggests \(\ln(x^{2} + 4)\).

stem: The region R is enclosed by the \(y\)-axis, the \(x\)-axis, the line \(y = 2\) and the curve \(y = \sqrt{x - 1}\). It lies to the left of the curve, between \(y = 0\) and \(y = 2\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write \(x\) in terms of \(y\) for this curve.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write down an integral, with respect to \(y\), for the area of R.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the exact area of R.

idea: R lies between the \(y\)-axis and the curve, so it is easier to slice it horizontally: each strip has length \(x\) and thickness \(dy\), and \(y\) runs from 0 to 2.

solution.label: b
steps: Integrate the horizontal distance from the \(y\)-axis to the curve.

stem: A wood turner makes a table leg by rotating the curve \(y = 3 - 0.5\sin\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)\), for \(0 \le x \le 20\), through \(360^{\circ}\) about the \(x\)-axis. Lengths are in cm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down an integral for the volume of the leg.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the volume of the leg.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The wood has a density of 0.7 g cm⁻³. Find the mass of the leg.

idea: Volume of revolution about the \(x\)-axis: \(V = \pi\displaystyle\int_{a}^{b} y^{2}\,dx\), adding up thin discs of radius \(y\).

stem: The inside of a glass is formed by rotating the part of the curve \(y = 0.5x^{2}\) between \(y = 0\) and \(y = 4.5\) through \(360^{\circ}\) about the \(y\)-axis. Lengths are in cm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the glass holds \(20.25\pi\) cm³.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the depth of liquid when the glass holds half of its volume.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Juice is poured in at 5 cm³ s⁻¹. Find the rate at which the level is rising when the depth is 2 cm.

idea: About the \(y\)-axis, \(V = \pi\displaystyle\int x^{2}\,dy\), so first write \(x^{2}\) in terms of \(y\). For depth \(h\), the volume is \(V(h) = \pi\displaystyle\int_{0}^{h} x^{2}\,dy\), and \(\dfrac{dV}{dt} = \dfrac{dV}{dh}\dfrac{dh}{dt}\).

solution.label: b
steps: For depth \(h\), \(V = \pi h^{2}\). Half full: \(\pi h^{2} = 10.125\pi\), so \(h = \sqrt{10.125} = 3.181\ldots\)

stem: A leaf-shaped logo is the region between the curves \(y = \sin x\) and \(y = 0.3x(\pi - x)\), for \(0 \le x \le \pi\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the curves meet at \(x = 0\) and \(x = \pi\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine which curve is above the other between these points.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the exact area of the logo.

idea: Area between curves \(= \displaystyle\int (\text{upper} - \text{lower})\,dx\). Check one value of \(x\) in between to see which curve is on top.

solution.label: a
steps: At \(x = 0\) and \(x = \pi\), both \(\sin x\) and \(0.3x(\pi - x)\) are 0.

solution.label: b
steps: At \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\): \(\sin x = 1\) and \(0.3 \times \dfrac{\pi}{2} \times \dfrac{\pi}{2} = 0.740\ldots\) (and the curves do not meet in between).

stem: A napkin ring is made by rotating the region inside the circle \(x^{2} + y^{2} = 25\) and above the line \(y = 3\) through \(360^{\circ}\) about the \(x\)-axis. Lengths are in cm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the \(x\)-coordinates where the line meets the circle.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write down an integral for the volume of the ring.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the exact volume of the ring.

idea: Each slice of the solid is a washer: a disc of radius \(\sqrt{25 - x^{2}}\) with a hole of radius 3. Its area is \(\pi(R^{2} - r^{2})\).

stem: A robot vacuum moves back and forth along a straight skirting board. Its velocity is \(v(t) = 0.3t^{2} - 1.2t + 0.9\) m s⁻¹, for \(0 \le t \le 4\) seconds.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the acceleration of the robot at \(t = 2\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the times when the robot is at rest.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the total distance travelled in the 4 seconds.

idea: Acceleration is \(\dfrac{dv}{dt}\). Distance is \(\displaystyle\int |v|\,dt\): the robot reverses when \(v = 0\), so add the distances of each stage.

stem: A kayak drifts backwards in a current and then paddles forwards along a straight river bank. Its velocity is \(v(t) = 2 - 3e^{-0.5t}\) m s⁻¹, for \(t \ge 0\) seconds.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down the initial velocity.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the exact time at which the kayak changes direction.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the displacement of the kayak after 4 seconds.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the distance travelled by the kayak in the first 4 seconds.

idea: Displacement is \(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{4} v\,dt\), where backward motion cancels forward motion. Distance is \(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{4}|v|\,dt\), where it does not.

solution.label: d
steps: \(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{4}|2 - 3e^{-0.5t}|\,dt = 3.568\ldots\) by calculator (the kayak goes back about 0.378 m first).

stem: A test sled runs along a straight rail. Its acceleration is \(a(t) = 6 - 2t\) m s⁻², for \(0 \le t \le 6\) seconds. At \(t = 0\) its velocity is \(-7\) m s⁻¹ and its displacement from the start is 0.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find an expression for the velocity \(v(t)\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the exact times at which the sled is at rest.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the displacement of the sled at \(t = 6\).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the total distance travelled by the sled.

idea: Integrate the acceleration to get velocity, and use \(v(0) = -7\) to find the constant. Integrate again for displacement.

stem: A speed skater starts from rest. Her speed \(t\) seconds after the start is modelled by \(v(t) = 14(1 - e^{-0.6t})\) m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find her acceleration at the start.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the time at which she reaches 95 % of her top (limiting) speed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the time she takes to skate 500 m.

idea: As \(t\) grows, \(e^{-0.6t} \to 0\), so the top speed is 14 m s⁻¹. The distance after \(T\) seconds is \(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{T} v\,dt\); set it equal to 500 and solve with the calculator.

stem: A loaf of bread comes out of the oven at 90 °C into a kitchen at 20 °C. The rate at which its temperature \(T\) °C falls is proportional to the difference between \(T\) and the kitchen temperature. Time \(t\) is in minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down a differential equation for \(T\), using a constant \(k > 0\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: For this loaf, \(k = 0.05\). Show that \(T = 20 + 70e^{-0.05t}\) satisfies your equation and the starting temperature.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the temperature of the loaf after 15 minutes.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the exact time at which the loaf reaches 30 °C.

idea: ‘Proportional to the difference’ gives \(\dfrac{dT}{dt} = -k(T - 20)\); the minus sign is there because the temperature falls. To check a solution, differentiate it and compare both sides.

solution.label: a
steps: The loaf is hotter than the kitchen, so \(T\) decreases.

stem: Consider the differential equation \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 3x^{2}(y + 1)\), for \(y > -1\), with \(y = 1\) when \(x = 0\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use separation of variables to find \(y\) in terms of \(x\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the value of \(y\) when \(x = 1\).

idea: Put all the \(y\) terms on one side and all the \(x\) terms on the other: \(\displaystyle\int \dfrac{1}{y + 1}\,dy = \int 3x^{2}\,dx\). Use the initial condition to find the constant.

stem: When a promotion ends, the number of active users \(N\) of an app falls. A model is \(\dfrac{dN}{dt} = -\dfrac{0.6N}{t + 1}\), where \(t\) is the time in weeks after the promotion ends, and \(N = 5000\) when \(t = 0\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Solve the differential equation to show that \(N = 5000(t + 1)^{-0.6}\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the number of active users 9 weeks after the promotion ends.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find when the number of active users falls to 1000.

idea: Separate: \(\displaystyle\int \dfrac{dN}{N} = \int -\dfrac{0.6}{t + 1}\,dt\). Both sides give logarithms; use \(a\ln b = \ln b^{a}\) to tidy the result.

stem: The number of fish \(P\) in a fish farm changes according to \(\dfrac{dP}{dt} = 0.05P - 200\), where \(t\) is in years. The term 200 is the number of fish harvested each year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the equilibrium population, and explain what it means.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Given that \(P = 5000\) when \(t = 0\), use separation of variables to show that \(P = 4000 + 1000e^{0.05t}\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: A second farm follows the same model but starts with \(P = 3000\) when \(t = 0\), so that \(P = 4000 - 1000e^{0.05t}\). Find when the second farm runs out of fish.

idea: At equilibrium \(\dfrac{dP}{dt} = 0\). Separate as \(\displaystyle\int \dfrac{dP}{0.05P - 200} = \int dt\); the integral on the left is \(\dfrac{1}{0.05}\ln|0.05P - 200|\).

solution.label: a
solution.answer: \(P = 4000\): the natural growth exactly replaces the fish harvested, so the population stays the same

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the gradient of the solution curve that passes through \((1, 3)\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write down the equation of the line on which every slope is horizontal.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Show that \(y = x - 1\) is a solution of the differential equation.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Describe the shape of the solution curve through \((0, 2)\) as \(x\) increases, and state the line it approaches.

idea: The gradient at any point is \(x - y\). A line is a solution if its gradient equals \(x - y\) at every point on it. Follow the little segments from \((0, 2)\) to see where the curve goes.

solution.label: c
solution.answer: Both sides equal 1, so it is a solution

solution.label: d
steps: At \((0, 2)\) the gradient is \(-2\), so the curve falls at first, crosses \(y = x\) where its gradient is 0, then rises. Above \(y = x - 1\) the slopes are less than 1, so the curve gets closer to that line but cannot cross it.
(The general solution is \(y = x - 1 + Ce^{-x}\); here \(C = 3\).)
solution.answer: It falls to a minimum, then rises and gets closer and closer to the line \(y = x - 1\) from above

stem: A spherical water droplet evaporates. Its volume \(V\) decreases at a rate proportional to its surface area \(A\): \(\dfrac{dV}{dt} = -kA\), where \(k > 0\). For a sphere of radius \(r\), \(V = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^{3}\) and \(A = 4\pi r^{2}\). Lengths are in mm and time in seconds.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that \(\dfrac{dr}{dt} = -k\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: The radius falls from 2 mm to 1.4 mm in 30 seconds. Find \(k\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find how long it takes for the droplet to evaporate completely, starting from a radius of 2 mm.

idea: Use the chain rule: \(\dfrac{dV}{dt} = \dfrac{dV}{dr}\dfrac{dr}{dt}\), and notice that \(\dfrac{dV}{dr}\) is exactly the surface area.

solution.label: a
steps: \(\dfrac{dV}{dt} = 4\pi r^{2}\dfrac{dr}{dt}\), and this equals \(-k \times 4\pi r^{2}\). Divide by \(4\pi r^{2}\).

solution.label: b
steps: The radius falls at a constant rate: \(\dfrac{2 - 1.4}{30}\).

stem: Consider \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = x + y^{2}\), with \(y = 0.5\) when \(x = 0\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use Euler's method with a step length of 0.1 to find an approximate value of \(y\) when \(x = 0.3\). Show each step.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one way to make the approximation more accurate.

idea: Euler's method: \(y_{n+1} = y_{n} + h\,f(x_{n}, y_{n})\) and \(x_{n+1} = x_{n} + h\). Keep full calculator accuracy from step to step.

solution.label: b
steps: A smaller step follows the curve more closely.

stem: A ball bearing is dropped into a tall jar of oil. Its velocity \(v\) m s⁻¹ after \(t\) seconds satisfies \(\dfrac{dv}{dt} = 9.8 - 2v\), with \(v = 0\) when \(t = 0\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use Euler's method with step length 0.1 to estimate \(v\) when \(t = 0.3\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that \(v = 4.9(1 - e^{-2t})\) is the exact solution.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the percentage error in your estimate from part (a).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why Euler's method overestimates \(v\) here.

idea: Each Euler step uses the gradient at the start of the step. Here the gradient \(9.8 - 2v\) gets smaller as \(v\) grows, so the start-of-step gradient is always too big.

solution.label: d
steps: The acceleration decreases as \(v\) increases, but each step uses the larger value from the start of the step.
solution.answer: The gradient decreases during each step, so using its starting value overshoots

stem: In a greenhouse, \(x\) aphids are eaten by \(y\) ladybirds. A model is
\[\dfrac{dx}{dt} = 0.3x - 0.002xy, \qquad \dfrac{dy}{dt} = -0.2y + 0.001xy,\]
where \(t\) is in days. At \(t = 0\) there are 220 aphids and 60 ladybirds.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use Euler's method with step length 0.5 to estimate the numbers of aphids and ladybirds after 1 day.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the equilibrium point with \(x > 0\) and \(y > 0\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain what this equilibrium means for the greenhouse.

idea: For a coupled system, update both variables in each step using the old values of both: \(x_{n+1} = x_{n} + h\dfrac{dx}{dt}\) and \(y_{n+1} = y_{n} + h\dfrac{dy}{dt}\), with both rates found from \((x_{n}, y_{n})\).

solution.label: c
solution.answer: With 200 aphids and 150 ladybirds, both numbers stay the same

stem: A buoy bobs up and down in still water. Its displacement \(x\) m above its resting level, \(t\) seconds after it is released, satisfies \(\dfrac{d^{2}x}{dt^{2}} + 0.4\dfrac{dx}{dt} + 4x = 0\), with \(x = 1\) and \(\dfrac{dx}{dt} = 0\) when \(t = 0\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Let \(v = \dfrac{dx}{dt}\). Write the equation as a system of two first-order differential equations, and in matrix form.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use Euler's method with step length 0.1 to estimate \(x\) and \(v\) when \(t = 0.2\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the eigenvalues of the matrix in part (a), and explain what they show about the motion of the buoy.

idea: A second-order equation becomes two first-order ones: \(\dot{x} = v\) and \(\dot{v} = -4x - 0.4v\). Complex eigenvalues mean oscillation; a negative real part means the oscillation dies away.

solution.label: c
solution.answer: \(\lambda = -0.2 \pm 1.99i\): the buoy oscillates (imaginary part) with decreasing amplitude (negative real part), settling at its resting level

stem: Consider the system \(\dfrac{dx}{dt} = 4x - 2y\), \(\dfrac{dy}{dt} = x + y\), with \(x = 3\) and \(y = 2\) when \(t = 0\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down the matrix \(\boldsymbol{A}\) such that \(\begin{pmatrix}\dot{x} \\ \dot{y}\end{pmatrix} = \boldsymbol{A}\begin{pmatrix}x \\ y\end{pmatrix}\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the eigenvalues of \(\boldsymbol{A}\) and a corresponding eigenvector for each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Hence find \(x\) and \(y\) in terms of \(t\).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Describe the long-term behaviour of the solution.

idea: The general solution is \(c_{1}e^{\lambda_{1}t}\boldsymbol{v}_{1} + c_{2}e^{\lambda_{2}t}\boldsymbol{v}_{2}\). At \(t = 0\) the exponentials are 1, so the initial values give \(c_{1}\) and \(c_{2}\).

solution.label: a
steps: Read the coefficients row by row.

solution.label: d
steps: Both eigenvalues are positive, and \(e^{3t}\) grows fastest.
solution.answer: \(x\) and \(y\) grow without limit, and the trajectory becomes parallel to \(\begin{pmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{pmatrix}\) (\(y \approx \tfrac{1}{2}x\))

stem: A greenhouse controller adjusts the temperature and humidity. Their deviations from the target values, \(x\) and \(y\), satisfy \(\dfrac{dx}{dt} = -x - 4y\), \(\dfrac{dy}{dt} = x - y\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the eigenvalues of the system's matrix.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the shape of the phase portrait, and state whether the controller brings the greenhouse back to its targets.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Determine whether the trajectories go round the origin clockwise or anticlockwise.

idea: Complex eigenvalues \(a \pm bi\) give spirals: inwards if \(a < 0\), outwards if \(a > 0\). To find the direction, work out the velocity vector at a convenient point such as \((1, 0)\).

solution.label: b
steps: The real part \(-1\) is negative and the imaginary part is not 0.
solution.answer: Trajectories spiral in towards the origin (a stable spiral), so the deviations die away and the targets are restored

solution.label: c
steps: At \((1, 0)\): \(\dfrac{dx}{dt} = -1\), \(\dfrac{dy}{dt} = 1\). On the positive \(x\)-axis the motion is upwards (and to the left).

stem: The deviations \(x\) and \(y\) of two interacting populations from their equilibrium levels satisfy \(\dfrac{dx}{dt} = x + 3y\), \(\dfrac{dy}{dt} = 3x + y\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the eigenvalues and corresponding eigenvectors of the system's matrix.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the type of equilibrium at the origin.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe the starting points from which the populations return to equilibrium.

idea: Real eigenvalues of opposite signs give a saddle: motion along the eigenvector with the negative eigenvalue heads into the origin; any part along the other eigenvector grows.

solution.label: b
steps: One positive and one negative eigenvalue.

solution.label: c
steps: The solution is \(c_{1}e^{4t}\begin{pmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{pmatrix} + c_{2}e^{-2t}\begin{pmatrix}1 \\ -1\end{pmatrix}\); it tends to the origin only if \(c_{1} = 0\).
solution.answer: Only starting points on the line \(y = -x\)

stem: Each system below has the form \(\begin{pmatrix}\dot{x} \\ \dot{y}\end{pmatrix} = \boldsymbol{A}\begin{pmatrix}x \\ y\end{pmatrix}\). For each, find the eigenvalues of \(\boldsymbol{A}\) and state the type of equilibrium at the origin.

parts.label: a
parts.text: \(\boldsymbol{A} = \begin{pmatrix}-3 & 1 \\ 0 & -2\end{pmatrix}\)

parts.label: b
parts.text: \(\boldsymbol{A} = \begin{pmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -2\end{pmatrix}\)

parts.label: c
parts.text: \(\boldsymbol{A} = \begin{pmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{pmatrix}\)

idea: Two negative real eigenvalues: stable node (sink). Opposite signs: saddle. Complex with positive real part: unstable spiral (spirals outwards).

solution.label: a
steps: The matrix is triangular, so the eigenvalues are its diagonal entries.
